panels.title: Big questions
points: Why do stories of enchantment so often end in loss?
What does a person reveal about themselves without meaning to?
Do people far from a war really care?
Can a single word make someone feel less than whole?

panels.title: Islamic foundation
panels.text: The Prophet ﷺ taught in his farewell sermon that no Arab is superior to a non-Arab, nor a white person to a black person, except by righteousness (Musnad Ahmad). Labels that make anyone 'less' have no place in Islam.

keywords.def: a story told in short, usually four-line stanzas
a story told inside another story
a period valuing emotion, nature and imagination
being open to more than one meaning
a poem spoken by one character to a silent listener
a sentence running on over a line break
when the reader understands more than the speaker
placing two contrasting things side by side
a group of words linked by topic
a dark room where photographs are developed
the way a language is spoken in a particular community
speaking straight to the listener with 'you'

panels.title: La Belle Dame sans Merci (Keats): the ballad, the frame and enchantment
points: Stanzas 1 to 3: a questioner finds a pale, lonely knight
Stanzas 4 to 12: the knight tells his tale
He met a lady, 'a faery's child', and was enchanted
He dreamed of pale kings and woke alone on the hill

panels.title: My Last Duchess (Browning): power, control and the dramatic monologue
points: The Duke of Ferrara shows a portrait of his late wife
His listener is an envoy arranging his next marriage
He complains she smiled too freely at everyone
Then he moves on to the dowry and a bronze statue

panels.title: War Photographer (Carol Ann Duffy): witness, memory and indifference
points: A war photographer develops his films alone in his darkroom
He is home in England after photographing war
He remembers what he saw
His editor will choose a few images for a Sunday supplement

panels.title: Half-caste (Agard): voice, identity and challenging language
points: The speaker challenges someone who calls him 'half-caste'
He mocks the word with absurd comparisons
Painters mix colours; English weather mixes sun and cloud
He ends inviting the listener to see 'de whole' of him

panels.title: Do not go gentle into that good night (Thomas): the villanelle and the fight against death
points: 19 lines: five tercets and a final quatrain
Two refrains alternate, then join at the end
Only two rhyme sounds throughout
Written 1951, to the poet's dying father

panels.title: Remember (Rossetti): the sonnet, the volta and the gift of forgetting
points: Octave: 'Remember me', repeated as a plea
Volta at line 9: 'Yet if you should forget me for a while'
Sestet: do not grieve if you forget
A gentle, selfless change of heart

panels.title: Poem at Thirty-Nine (Walker): memory, a parent and becoming yourself
points: An adult speaker, aged thirty-nine, remembers her late father
Opens: 'How I miss my father.'
Ordinary tasks (money, cooking) bring him back
She imagines him seeing the woman she has become

panels.title: The Tyger (Blake): questions, creation and awe
points: Hammer, chain, furnace, anvil
Creation as hard, fiery labour
Questions pile up stanza by stanza
Last stanza repeats the first, with 'Dare' for 'Could'

panels.title: How does Keats present the effect of enchantment?
points: Point: enchantment leaves the knight drained and stuck
Evidence: 'Alone and palely loitering'
Technique: ballad frame and repeated opening
Zoom: 'loitering' suggests aimless waiting with nowhere to go

Answer: Keats presents enchantment as draining: the knight is 'Alone and palely loitering', and 'loitering' suggests he waits without purpose; because the final stanza returns to these words, the ballad frame traps him in his loss.

panels.title: How does Browning present the Duke's need for control?
points: Point: the Duke treats his wife as a possession
Evidence: 'my last Duchess'
Technique: possessive pronoun; dramatic monologue
Zoom: 'last' suggests she is one of a series, replaceable

Answer: Browning presents the Duke as possessive from the first words: 'my last Duchess' turns a wife into an item in a collection, and 'last' hints she has been replaced; perhaps, though, his need to control betrays insecurity.

panels.title: How does Duffy present the photographer's feelings?
points: Point: Duffy presents a man burdened by what he has seen
Evidence: 'spools of suffering set out in ordered rows'
Technique: alliteration; religious imagery
Zoom: 'ordered' shows his calm control over chaos

Answer: Duffy presents the photographer as burdened but controlled: the sibilant 'spools of suffering set out in ordered rows' turns horror into neat lines, and 'ordered' suggests the calm he must keep, though perhaps it is also numbness.

panels.title: Compare how the poets present voice and power.
points: Point: both poems are spoken by one voice to a silent listener
Evidence: 'my last Duchess' / 'Explain yuself'
Methods: smooth, controlling couplets vs free, challenging dialect
Analysis: the Duke uses voice to dominate; Agard's speaker to resist

Answer: Both poems are monologues to a silent listener, but their voices work in opposite directions: the Duke's polished couplets ('my last Duchess') use language to own and silence, whereas Agard's dialect demands 'Explain yuself', using language to resist a label and claim his whole identity.
